Tampered PushEngage SDK fetched from clientcdn.pushengage.com during exposure window AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for endpoints (or web servers acting as origin scrapers) that downloaded pushengage-web-sdk.js or pushengage-subscription.js from clientcdn.pushengage.com between 2026-06-12 and 2026-06-14 UTC, the window in which Sansec observed the tampered script being served. Rationale: The article (and PushEngage's own incident notice) name the two specific JS filenames and the exact CDN host. Bounding the search to 2026-06-12 → 2026-06-14 UTC matches the Sansec-published exposure window so legitimate post-cleanup loads do not trigger. Cross-checked against: • https://sansec.io/research/wordpress-plugin-supply-chain • https://www.pushengage.com/incident-report-june-2026/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1189
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WordPress site visitors who happened to load the SDK after the CDN cache was already cleared but before stale CDN edge nodes refreshed (PushEngage notes some servers still served it into June 14)
  • Web-scraping monitoring infra (Synthetics, Catchpoint) replaying the URL for availability checks
  • Security researchers downloading both filenames for analysis from corporate workstations
  • Internal CDN-cache invalidation tooling re-fetching the asset to populate replacement copies
Response runbook
1. Triage — confirm whether the downloading endpoint is a WordPress admin browser session (high impact) versus a content-rendering visitor browser (low impact). Pull the SHA256 of the cached JS to compare to PushEngage's clean hash. 2. Contain — if an admin browser loaded the tampered file, force-logout all WordPress administrators on the affected site, rotate WP salts in wp-config.php, and invalidate session cookies. 3. Hunt — pivot to the C2 detection (tidio.cc / 84.201.6.54) for the same DeviceId, enumerate users for developer_api1 or dev_xxxxxx, and inspect wp-content/plugins for content-delivery-helper or database-optimizer folders.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp between (datetime(2026-06-12T00:00:00Z) .. datetime(2026-06-14T23:59:59Z))
| where RemoteUrl has "clientcdn.pushengage.com"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("pushengage-web-sdk.js", "pushengage-subscription.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let WindowStart = datetime(2026-06-12T00:00:00Z);
let WindowEnd = datetime(2026-06-14T23:59:59Z);
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated between (WindowStart .. WindowEnd)
| where (RequestURL has "clientcdn.pushengage.com") and (RequestURL has_any ("pushengage-web-sdk.js","pushengage-subscription.js"))
| project TimeGenerated, Host=SourceHostName, SrcIP=SourceIP, URL=RequestURL, UserAgent=RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor),
(ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated between (WindowStart .. WindowEnd)
| where (Url has "clientcdn.pushengage.com") and (Url has_any ("pushengage-web-sdk.js","pushengage-subscription.js"))
| project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, SrcIP=SrcIpAddr, URL=Url, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DeviceVendor=EventVendor),
(W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated between (WindowStart .. WindowEnd)
| where csUriStem has_any ("pushengage-web-sdk.js","pushengage-subscription.js")
| project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, SrcIP=cIP, URL=strcat(csUriStem, "?", csUriQuery), UserAgent=csUserAgent, DeviceVendor="IIS")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rogue WordPress admin account created matching developer_api1 / dev_xxxxxx AIInstallation High
Hunts for the Sansec-published rogue WordPress admin usernames (developer_api1 or anything matching dev_<6char>) appearing in identity / auth / web-server logs. The backdoor JS used the logged-in admin's session to create this account silently. Rationale: Sansec's IoC table explicitly lists 'developer_api1' and the pattern 'dev_xxxxxx' as the rogue admin usernames. These strings should not appear in any legitimate WordPress site's auth or web logs, making string-match detections high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://sansec.io/research/wordpress-plugin-supply-chain
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1098
Data sourcesChange.Account_Management Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developer accounts coincidentally matching dev_<6char> naming (rare but possible at large hosting providers)
  • Threat-intel feeds / IOC ingestion pipelines emitting the username string in their own log lines
  • Security scanner (Wordfence, Sucuri) producing reports that include the rogue username for awareness
  • WordPress plugins that store the username verbatim in their changelog or admin notice
Response runbook
1. Triage — confirm the source site is one of the affected plugins (PushEngage, OptinMonster, TrustPulse) and pull the wp_users row for developer_api1 / matching dev_* accounts including user_registered timestamp. 2. Contain — delete the rogue admin account, rotate all administrator passwords + WP secret salts in wp-config.php, and invalidate active sessions via wp user session destroy --all. 3. Hunt — check wp-content/plugins for content-delivery-helper or database-optimizer directories, pivot to outbound traffic to tidio.cc / 84.201.6.54, and rotate the CDN API key + database credentials.
union
(DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\wp-content\" or FolderPath has "/wp-content/"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("developer_api1", "dev_")),
(DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("developer_api1", "INSERT INTO wp_users", "wp_insert_user")
  and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)dev_[a-z0-9]{4,8}")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csUriStem has_any ("/wp-admin/user-new.php","/wp-admin/users.php","/wp-json/wp/v2/users","/xmlrpc.php")
| where csUriQuery has_any ("developer_api1","dev_") or csUriStem has "developer_api1"
| project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, SrcIP=cIP, URL=strcat(csUriStem,"?",csUriQuery), Method=csMethod, UA=csUserAgent),
(Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("developer_api1","wp_insert_user")
   or SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)\bdev_[a-z0-9]{4,8}\b"
| project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, ProcessName, Message=SyslogMessage),
(CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RequestURL has_any ("developer_api1","/wp-json/wp/v2/users","/wp-admin/user-new.php")
| project TimeGenerated, Host=SourceHostName, SrcIP=SourceIP, URL=RequestURL, Method=RequestMethod)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Suspicious WordPress plugin folder created (content-delivery-helper / database-optimizer) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the Sansec-named hidden-plugin directories that the backdoor installs under wp-content/plugins. These plugin folder names are not associated with any legitimate WordPress plugin and represent the in-tree web shell. Rationale: The article quotes Sansec's IOC list naming exactly two backdoor plugin folders: content-delivery-helper ('Content Delivery Helper') and database-optimizer ('Database Optimizer'). Neither matches any plugin in the WordPress.org repository, so file-create events under those subpaths are nearly noise-free. Cross-checked against: • https://sansec.io/research/wordpress-plugin-supply-chain
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Forensic analyst extracting a tarball of the compromised plugin folder onto a sandbox host for analysis
  • Backup-restore process replaying historical file events into the SIEM after a clean-up
  • Custom internal plugin coincidentally named 'database-optimizer' in a hosting provider's site template (rare — verify by SHA256 against known-good hashes)
  • Wordfence / Sucuri scanner quarantining the backdoor and producing its own file-event records
Response runbook
1. Triage — confirm the host is a WordPress web server and the directory path actually exists on disk. Capture file listing + SHA256 of the PHP files in those folders. 2. Contain — quarantine the entire wp-content/plugins/<folder>/ directory tree (do not delete; preserve for forensics), block the host's egress to tidio.cc and 84.201.6.54, and disable the wp-admin endpoint pending review. 3. Hunt — enumerate wp_users for developer_api1 / dev_* accounts, search for any other PHP files modified in the same minute window across wp-content, and check web-server access logs for the web-shell URL by correlating against subsequent outbound POSTs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileRenamed", "FileModified")
| where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)[\\/]wp-content[\\/]plugins[\\/](content-delivery-helper|database-optimizer)[\\/]"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
let Suspicious = dynamic(["content-delivery-helper","database-optimizer"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)[\\/]wp-content[\\/]plugins[\\/](content-delivery-helper|database-optimizer)[\\/]"
| project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, Actor=ActorUsername, FilePath=TargetFilePath, Process=ActingProcessName, Cmd=ActingProcessCommandLine, Hash=TargetFileSHA256),
(Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any (Suspicious) and SyslogMessage has "wp-content/plugins/"
| project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, Actor="", FilePath=SyslogMessage, Process=ProcessName, Cmd="", Hash="")
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Sansec hidden WordPress plugin directory (content-delivery-helper / database-optimizer)
id: 7c4d5e6f-3a2b-4c7d-9e1f-2b3a4c5d6e03
description: Detects creation of the hidden-plugin directories installed by the tampered PushEngage / OptinMonster / TrustPulse scripts (Sansec, June 2026). These directories carry the web shell that does not surface in the WordPress dashboard.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/popular-wordpress-plugin-scripts.html
author: thn-usecases
date: 2026/06/15
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1505.003
  - attack.t1195.002
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '/wp-content/plugins/content-delivery-helper/'
      - '/wp-content/plugins/database-optimizer/'
      - '\wp-content\plugins\content-delivery-helper\'
      - '\wp-content\plugins\database-optimizer\'
  condition: selection
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon OR source:linux.auditd OR source:windows.defender) AND (@TargetFilename:(*\/wp-content\/plugins\/content-delivery-helper\/* OR *\/wp-content\/plugins\/database-optimizer\/* OR *\\wp-content\\plugins\\content-delivery-helper\\* OR *\\wp-content\\plugins\\database-optimizer\\*) OR @file.path:(*\/wp-content\/plugins\/content-delivery-helper\/* OR *\/wp-content\/plugins\/database-optimizer\/*))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/[\\\/]wp-content[\\\/]plugins[\\\/](content-delivery-helper|database-optimizer)[\\\/]/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.user) as user values(Filesystem.process_name) as process from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*/wp-content/plugins/content-delivery-helper/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/wp-content/plugins/database-optimizer/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\wp-content\\plugins\\content-delivery-helper\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\wp-content\\plugins\\database-optimizer\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.user) as user values(Filesystem.process_name) as process from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*/wp-content/plugins/content-delivery-helper/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/wp-content/plugins/database-optimizer/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\wp-content\\plugins\\content-delivery-helper\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\wp-content\\plugins\\database-optimizer\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
WordPress PHP process spawning shell from wp-content directory AIExploitation Medium
Detects php / php-fpm / php-cgi processes whose working directory or invoking script path resolves under wp-content spawning cmd.exe / powershell.exe / bash / sh — the canonical web-shell execution shape for the hidden Sansec backdoor. Rationale: The article says the hidden plugin opens a web shell — 'anyone who knows the right URL can run code on the server.' On a WordPress host, that materialises as php / php-fpm spawning a shell or curl/wget. Anchoring on the wp-content / wp-admin path eliminates generic PHP CLI scripts. Cross-checked against: • https://sansec.io/research/wordpress-plugin-supply-chain
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WordPress CLI tools (wp-cli) running maintenance tasks that legitimately spawn curl for plugin updates
  • Backup plugins (UpdraftPlus, BackupBuddy) shelling out to tar/gzip from wp-content/uploads
  • Image-processing plugins invoking imagemagick / ffmpeg via shell wrappers
  • Cron-scheduled WordPress jobs that pull remote feeds via curl from wp-content paths
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-cli","updraftplus","backupbuddy","wp-cron.php") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("tar","gzip","rsync"))
Response runbook
1. Triage — capture the full process chain (grandparent → parent → child) and the script path resolved from the PHP CLI args. Identify which WordPress plugin owns the parent path. 2. Contain — kill the offending PHP worker, quarantine the parent script file, and add a temporary egress block for the host to tidio.cc / 84.201.6.54. 3. Hunt — pivot on the same DeviceId for content-delivery-helper / database-optimizer folder writes, rogue developer_api1 / dev_* admin accounts, and inbound HTTP requests for the script path in web-server access logs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php.exe","php-cgi.exe","php-fpm","php")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","sh","dash","zsh","nc","ncat","curl.exe","wget.exe")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("base64 -d", "FromBase64String", "eval(", "system(", "passthru(")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("wp-content","wp-admin","wp-includes")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-content","wp-admin")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(^|[\\/])php(-cgi|-fpm)?(\.exe)?$"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(^|[\\/])(cmd\.exe|powershell\.exe|pwsh\.exe|bash|sh|dash|zsh|nc|ncat|curl(\.exe)?|wget(\.exe)?)$"
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("base64 -d","FromBase64String","eval(","system(","passthru(")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-content","wp-admin","wp-includes")
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-content","wp-admin")
| project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, Actor=ActorUsername,
          Parent=ParentProcessName, ParentCmd=ParentProcessCommandLine,
          Child=ActingProcessName, ChildCmd=ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PHP process spawning shell from WordPress directory
id: 8e5d6f7a-4b3c-4d8e-9a2f-3c4d5e6f7a04
description: Detects php / php-fpm / php-cgi spawning a shell or download utility while running with wp-content/wp-admin/wp-includes in its path or command line — the canonical Sansec backdoor web-shell execution pattern.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/popular-wordpress-plugin-scripts.html
author: thn-usecases
date: 2026/06/15
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1505.003
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1059.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/php'
      - '/php-fpm'
      - '/php-cgi'
      - '\php.exe'
      - '\php-cgi.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/bash'
      - '/sh'
      - '/dash'
      - '/zsh'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\wget.exe'
  selection_path:
    ParentCommandLine|contains:
      - 'wp-content'
      - 'wp-admin'
      - 'wp-includes'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_path
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon OR source:linux.auditd) AND @ParentImage:(*\php.exe OR *\PHP.EXE OR */php OR */php-fpm OR */php-cgi) AND @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\CMD.EXE OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR */bash OR */sh OR */dash OR */curl OR */wget OR *\curl.exe OR *\wget.exe) AND @ParentCommandLine:(*wp-content* OR *wp-admin* OR *wp-includes*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^php(-cgi|-fpm)?(\.exe)?$/i
| ImageFileName=/(cmd\.exe|powershell\.exe|pwsh\.exe|[\\\/](bash|sh|dash|zsh|nc|ncat|curl|wget))(\.exe)?$/i
| regex("(?i)(wp-content|wp-admin|wp-includes)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("php.exe","php-cgi.exe","php-fpm","php")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","sh","dash","zsh","nc","ncat","curl","wget")) by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("php.exe","php-cgi.exe","php-fpm","php")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","sh","dash","zsh","nc","ncat","curl","wget")) by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-10795")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-10795")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-10795")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-10795")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'

        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'

falsepositives:

      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("84.201.6.54") or RemoteUrl has_any ("tidio.cc", "pushengage.com")

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Sniper Dz PhaaS infrastructure delivered via inbound email URLs · [LLM] User click-through on Sniper Dz redirect URL (Safe Links) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DNS or network egress to Sniper Dz infrastructure (IP and host indicators) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Sniper Dz PhaaS infrastructure delivered via inbound email URLs AIDelivery High
Inbound message contains a URL pointing to known Sniper Dz redirector or landing-page infrastructure (sniperdz.com, raviral.com, win.feezossl.xyz, etc.). Hunts the delivery vector even when the lure was originally posted on Facebook and forwarded to the victim via mail share. Group-IB tied these domains to the post-INTERPOL-takedown resurgence of the kit. Rationale: Uses the specific IOC domains the article enumerates as Sniper Dz infrastructure. Inbound + URL-domain match on a curated list is high-fidelity because these are not generic services; the only FP risk is a security analyst forwarding the IOC list internally.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1583.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst forwarding the IOC list or Group-IB write-up via email
  • Threat-intel digest emails that quote the URLs verbatim (Recorded Future, Group-IB newsletter)
  • Phishing-simulation vendor URLs that intentionally mimic these domains for awareness training
  • User reporting the phishing email back through a Report Phish add-in (causes the same URL to traverse the wire again)
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromAddress !endswith "@yourorg.com" and RecipientEmailAddress !in~ ("soc@yourorg.com","phishing-reports@yourorg.com","abuse@yourorg.com")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the full recipient list for the matching NetworkMessageId via EmailEvents and check whether any of them subsequently appear in UrlClickEvents for the same NetworkMessageId — that escalates this from delivery to click-through. Step 2 (contain): soft-delete or quarantine outstanding copies via Defender Threat Explorer for the NetworkMessageId, and add the matched UrlDomain values to the tenant block list. Step 3 (hunt): pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents/DnsEvents on the same domains for the last 14 days across the recipient population to find anyone who opened the URL outside Safe Links (clicked from mobile, copy-pasted into another browser).
let SniperDzDomains = dynamic(["sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | extend HostLower = tolower(UrlDomain)
    | where HostLower has_any (SniperDzDomains) or Url has_any (SniperDzDomains)
    | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain, ReportId
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, Url, UrlDomain
| order by Timestamp desc
let SniperDzDomains = dynamic(["sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor in~ ("Proofpoint","Mimecast","Cisco","Microsoft")
| where RequestURL has_any (SniperDzDomains) or DestinationHostName has_any (SniperDzDomains) or Message has_any (SniperDzDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DestinationHostName, Activity, DeviceAction, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

User click-through on Sniper Dz redirect URL (Safe Links) AIDelivery High
Safe Links UrlClickEvents for one of the Sniper Dz infrastructure domains, including ClickedThrough where the user bypassed the warning. This is the highest-fidelity post-delivery signal in the kill chain and the one that warrants immediate user contact, because the next step in the article's described funnel is browser-notification permission grant and TDS routing. Rationale: UrlClickEvents is the only Defender table that confirms the user actually opened the link (vs. it merely landed in their inbox). IsClickedThrough==true is an extra escalation signal because Safe Links warned them and they proceeded anyway — high-priority user-contact case. Domains are taken verbatim from the article's IOC list. Sentinel has no equivalent table without M365 Defender, so sentinel_kql is intentionally empty.
ATT&CKT1204.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst manually clicking the URL inside Safe Links during triage of UC1
  • Phishing-reporter user clicking the link before reporting (legitimate but operationally noisy)
  • Web-content categorisation services that crawl through Safe Links
  • Sandbox / detonation vendor accounts that follow URLs from quarantined mail
Suppression filter
| where AccountUpn !in~ ("soc-analyst@yourorg.com","ir-handler@yourorg.com") and IPAddress !in ("<known-sandbox-egress-ips>")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify AccountUpn and pull DeviceInfo to map to device; pull DeviceNetworkEvents on the user's primary device for the 30 min after ClickTime — look for follow-on traffic to the redirect chain or notification-service VAPID endpoints. Step 2 (contain): reset the user's session cookies for the mail tenant and force MFA re-prompt; if the user reports they granted browser-notification permission, push a managed-browser policy that revokes notification grants for the IOC domains. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the matched Url back to EmailEvents/EmailUrlInfo on the same NetworkMessageId to identify the original sender and other recipients; check for secondary clicks from the same campaign within 24h across the tenant.
let SniperDzDomains = dynamic(["sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io"]);
UrlClickEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
| extend UrlLower = tolower(Url)
| where UrlLower has_any (SniperDzDomains)
| join kind=leftouter (
    EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | project NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, Subject, RecipientEmailAddress
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, ActionType, IsClickedThrough, Workload, SenderFromAddress, Subject
| order by Timestamp desc

UrlClickEvents

| extend UrlLower = tolower(Url)
| where UrlLower has_any (SniperDzDomains)
| join kind=leftouter (
    EmailEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | project NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, Subject, RecipientEmailAddress
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, ActionType, IsClickedThrough, Workload, SenderFromAddress, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
DNS or network egress to Sniper Dz infrastructure (IP and host indicators) AICommand & Control Medium
Direct EDR/DNS observation of a workstation contacting one of the Sniper Dz hosting IPs (65.60.9.236, 108.178.23.118, 184.154.10.254) or attempting to resolve one of the named scam domains. Catches the case where the user reached the link outside Safe Links (mobile mail, SMS lure, Facebook in-app browser) and only the network egress survives. Rationale: Article enumerates three IPs (65.60.9.236, 108.178.23.118, 184.154.10.254) and nine domains as the campaign's hosting / redirect / TDS infrastructure. IP-membership + DNS-query-name match is the cleanest IOC pivot available and survives the scenario where Safe Links never observed the click (mobile, SMS lure, Facebook in-app browser).
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed ingestion box pulling the same IOCs from an OSINT source (e.g. abuse.ch fetch)
  • Researcher sandbox detonating the URLs from a corporate egress
  • URL-scanning service (urlscan, VirusTotal) called from an internal pipeline that resolves IOC domains
  • Pantheonsite.io is shared-tenant hosting — false positives possible if dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io is later reassigned to a legitimate customer (revalidate domain ownership quarterly)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in ("<threat-intel-sandbox-hostnames>") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe") | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-threatintel","svc-urlscan")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the device, the user, and the originating process — if InitiatingProcessFileName is a browser (msedge.exe/chrome.exe/firefox.exe) check UrlClickEvents and EmailEvents for the same user within the prior 30 min to identify the lure source; if it's a non-browser process, treat as elevated severity. Step 2 (contain): block the IPs at perimeter and the domains in the secure web gateway / DNS resolver; revoke browser notification permission via managed policy for affected users. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the user across DeviceNetworkEvents/DnsEvents for related redirect domains (Linktree / Linkbio destinations that ended in the same IPs), and across the wider population for any device that resolved any of the IOC domains in the last 30 days.
let SniperDzIPs = dynamic(["65.60.9.236","108.178.23.118","184.154.10.254"]);
let SniperDzDomains = dynamic(["sniperdz.com","raviral.com","offer.raviral.com","win.feezossl.xyz","win.anababayala.com","aff.bnaosf1he.shop","automaticgiveaway.000webhostapp.com","facebookbusiness0078.blogspot.be","dev-cdn370.pantheonsite.io"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in (SniperDzIPs)
   or (isnotempty(RemoteUrl) and tolower(RemoteUrl) has_any (SniperDzDomains))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc

  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:

let LookbackDays = 7d;

    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] GlobalProtect Gateway/Portal Traffic From CVE-2026-0257 Attack Infrastructure IPs
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] CVE-2026-0257 GlobalProtect PoC Client-Config Signature (Win10 Pro 64-bit + empty domain) · [LLM] GlobalProtect Session With CVE-2026-0257 PoC Default Hostnames (WINDOWS-LAPTOP-001 / DESKTOP-GP01 / GP-CLIENT) · [LLM] GlobalProtect Session Reporting Vendor-Default Placeholder MAC Address
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
CVE-2026-0257 GlobalProtect PoC Client-Config Signature (Win10 Pro 64-bit + empty domain) AIExploitation High
Hunts the article's primary detection guidance: successful GlobalProtect gateway-connected events whose client posture carries the hard-coded PoC values endpoint_os_version='Microsoft Windows 10 Pro 64-bit' AND empty source_user_info.domain. Real users almost never connect with both an empty domain and that exact Win10 Pro string simultaneously. Rationale: Uses the two PoC client-config strings Palo Alto Networks explicitly told customers to search for in GlobalProtect logs (endpoint_os_version='Microsoft Windows 10 Pro 64-bit' + empty source_user_info.domain). Both conditions together are essentially unique to the PoC. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/palo-alto-warns-of-active-exploitation.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication Network_Sessions.All_Sessions
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal pentest replay of the public PoC against a corporate GP gateway during an authorized assessment
  • Engineering test rigs imaged with a generic Win10 Pro template and joined to no AD domain (workgroup laptops)
  • Lab/QA GlobalProtect clients used by network engineers validating gateway upgrades with default client builds
  • Legitimate BYOD / contractor laptop running Windows 10 Pro never joined to a domain
Suppression filter
| where SourceUserName !in~ ('pentest-svc', 'redteam-lab', 'gp-test') | where SourceIP !in ('10.0.0.0/8', '192.168.0.0/16')
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SourceIP and SourceUserName from the hit and confirm whether the account is real, whether it normally connects from a domain-joined endpoint, and whether the source IP appears in the article's IOC list. 2) Contain: revoke active GlobalProtect sessions for the user, force a password+MFA reset, and block the source IP at the perimeter firewall pending investigation. Verify the appliance is patched against CVE-2026-0257. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP across firewall, IIS, and AAD logs for the past 60 days; look for additional gateway-connected events from the same IP under other usernames (credential spray pattern), and search internal traffic from the VPN-assigned IP for reconnaissance behaviour even though Palo Alto Networks reports no post-access activity yet.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DeviceVendor has 'Palo Alto'
| where DeviceProduct has 'GlobalProtect' or Message has 'GlobalProtect'
| where Message has 'gateway-connected'
| where Message has 'Microsoft Windows 10 Pro 64-bit'
| where Message has 'source_user_info.domain='
| where Message has_any ('source_user_info.domain=;', 'source_user_info.domain= ', 'source_user_info.domain=,', 'source_user_info.domain=|', 'source_user_info.domain=empty')
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DeviceAction, Activity, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GlobalProtect Gateway/Portal Traffic From CVE-2026-0257 Attack Infrastructure IPs AIDelivery Medium
Watches firewall + endpoint telemetry for any traffic involving the nine IP addresses Palo Alto Networks attributed to active CVE-2026-0257 exploitation. Hits represent either inbound exploitation attempts against your GP portal or outbound traffic from an internal host to the same infrastructure. Rationale: Direct hard match against the nine IOC IPs Palo Alto Networks published as confirmed CVE-2026-0257 attack infrastructure. Inbound hits = exploitation attempt; outbound from internal hosts = potential beacon to attacker infra. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/palo-alto-warns-of-active-exploitation.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • VPN-related troubleshooting / TAC support sessions where an engineer connects out to one of the IPs to validate the IOC list
  • Researcher / threat-hunter VM in your network actively probing the listed IPs for IOC enrichment
  • Stale NAT or shared-hosting reuse — one of the IPs is later assigned to a benign cloud customer your users legitimately reach
  • Honeypot or sandbox infrastructure your team operates that happens to share an IP range
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ('threathunter.exe', 'curl.exe', 'powershell_ise.exe') | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ('threat-research', 'soc-analyst')
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine direction — inbound to the GP portal or outbound from an internal endpoint. For inbound, confirm whether any of the same IPs produced a successful gateway-connected event in the last 30 days. For outbound, identify the source host and process. 2) Contain: block all nine IPs at the perimeter firewall and at any cloud egress gateway; if outbound, isolate the source endpoint immediately and preserve memory. 3) Hunt: search 60 days of firewall + proxy + DNS for any historical contact with these IPs; pull GlobalProtect logs for all successful gateway-connected events from these IPs and correlate to the PoC-signature detection above; check whether any of the source IPs probed other public services in your perimeter.

GlobalProtect Session With CVE-2026-0257 PoC Default Hostnames (WINDOWS-LAPTOP-001 / DESKTOP-GP01 / GP-CLIENT) AIExploitation High
Detects gateway-connected GlobalProtect events whose reported client hostname matches the three textbook PoC defaults disclosed by Palo Alto Networks. No real enterprise asset inventory contains these exact names. Rationale: These three hostnames are PoC scaffolding values explicitly named in the article's IOC list — they are functionally indistinguishable from canaries. A real client almost never reports these as its NetBIOS/host_id. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/palo-alto-warns-of-active-exploitation.html
ATT&CKT1133 T1190
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Newly imaged corporate laptop that hasn't received its asset-tag rename yet (rare; investigate anyway)
  • QA / staging GlobalProtect test client a network engineer named generically
  • Cloud-based VDI golden image whose hostname template literally happens to be DESKTOP-GP01
  • Asset built from an off-the-shelf Win10 install with the installer-generated default DESKTOP-XXXXXXX placeholder
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SourceIP and SourceUserName for each hit. Look up the username in IAM/HR — is the account active, and does the user own a real corporate laptop? Check whether the public_ip overlaps with the nine known attacker IPs. 2) Contain: kill the GP session, disable the account pending investigation, and block the source public IP. 3) Hunt: search 90 days for any prior gateway-connected event using the same hostname against any account; pivot on the SourceIP to find other compromised accounts; cross-check with the PoC-signature detection (Win10 Pro 64-bit + empty domain).
DeviceInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where DeviceName in~ ('WINDOWS-LAPTOP-001', 'DESKTOP-GP01', 'GP-CLIENT')
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, PublicIP, LoggedOnUsers, IsAzureADJoined
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor has 'Palo Alto'
| where Message has_any ('WINDOWS-LAPTOP-001', 'DESKTOP-GP01', 'GP-CLIENT')
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DeviceAction, Activity, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GlobalProtect Session Reporting Vendor-Default Placeholder MAC Address AIExploitation High
Hunts GlobalProtect HIP / host-info logs for the two textbook placeholder MAC addresses listed in the IOC bundle (aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff and 00:11:22:33:44:55). Real NICs ship with manufacturer-assigned OUIs; these values are unmistakable PoC artifacts. Rationale: Both MAC addresses are explicit IOCs from Palo Alto Networks' bundle and have OUIs that no real NIC manufacturer owns — aa:bb:cc and 00:11:22 are classic documentation/placeholder values used in the PoC client spoofing. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/palo-alto-warns-of-active-exploitation.html
ATT&CKT1133 T1036
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal pentester using a tool that doesn't randomise MACs and ships with the same documentation defaults
  • Network engineer running GlobalProtect from a Hyper-V/VirtualBox guest whose virtual NIC was assigned a manually-typed placeholder MAC during lab setup
  • Asset-management or HIP-misconfiguration where the agent fails to read the real MAC and falls back to a default
  • Threat-research VM in your environment that emulates the PoC client for IOC validation
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SourceIP, SourceUserName and timestamp for each hit. Confirm whether the same session also reported the PoC OS string or one of the cookie-cutter hostnames — multiple PoC indicators together is near-certain exploitation. 2) Contain: terminate the GP session, disable the account, block the source public IP, and force a credential reset. 3) Hunt: search 90 days for any other sessions reporting these MACs against any account; pivot on the public_ip to find sibling sessions; correlate against the PAN advisory for newer IOCs and confirm the appliance is patched against CVE-2026-0257.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor has 'Palo Alto'
| where Message has_any ('aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff', '00:11:22:33:44:55')
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DeviceAction, Activity, SourceMACAddress, DestinationMACAddress, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-0257")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-0257")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-0257")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

Actions on Objectives

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
